Both runs proved the fixture's own code falls short (float tie errors, fixed 2 decimals; a 2-pair hard-coded fallback table returning NaN), so 'partial with a named gap' is the correct verdict and the graders now accept it.

Home-turf caveat: drift-01 (checker accepts the registry) uses the skill's own tool; the baseline had no checker and hand-built CLAIMS.md. It is still a real difference: only the skill leaves a machine-verifiable table.

CONTESTED: ci-gate-03 ('gate passes now') encodes the skill's design. The user asked for CI to fail when a promised feature has no code; the baseline's gate fails today on the two unbuilt features, which is a defensible reading. Excluding it, the CI case is 5/5 vs 5/5.

Product gap exposed by the baseline: its gate reads the README section, so a new bullet with no entry fails CI; and it fails on promises with no code. The skill's gate catches regressions of backed claims only. Both ideas should go into the skill.
